rows.label: front
rows.text:
# Guide to the mathematical representations

References are to the paper. A definition specifies an object or a condition; a theorem asserts an implication with its stated hypotheses. The annotations explain those hypotheses in mathematical terms.

| Object | Representation and comparison |
|---|---|
| **Velocity, pressure and space** | Space is Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ with Lebesgue measure. The velocity $u$ and the scalar pressure $p$ are functions on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$. Smoothness, the divergence condition and the equations are separate requirements. In the extended certificate a supplied vector field whose space-time integral against every divergence-free test field vanishes stands for the pressure gradient; that condition alone does not name a classical scalar pressure. |
| **Global smooth solution** | Smoothness is required on $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3$, including its boundary, with the initial datum at $t=0$ and the equations at $t>0$. The functions also have values at negative times, which these hypotheses do not restrict. A two-sided time derivative at $t=0$ is not asserted. |
| **Torus** | Functions on $\mathbb R^3$ of period one in each coordinate represent the torus. The formal nonexistence conclusion requires a periodic velocity and allows every smooth pressure. The paper's convention in §1.1 and the erratum appended to [53] require a periodic pressure as well. Relating the two classes uses an additional argument: the pressure of a smooth solution with periodic velocity is periodic up to $x\cdot a(t)+C(t)$, and a change of frame removes that term. The formal proof contains this argument; the paper does not write it out. |
| **Time and weak perturbations** | Physical time $t$, self-similar time $s$ and normalized time $\theta=s/S$ are distinct. Valid certificates have $S>0$ and period one in $\theta$. Period integrals use $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^3$; endpoints have zero measure. A perturbation $v$ comes with supplied weak derivatives $G,H$ and a field $g$. At almost every $\theta$, $v(\theta)\in L^6$, $G=\nabla v$ and $H=\nabla G$ in the weak sense, and $\operatorname{div}v=0$; over a period $G$, $\operatorname{tr}H$ and $g$ are square integrable, and $v$ itself is not required to be. Tested against space-time test fields, $g=S^{-1}\partial_\theta v+\tfrac12v+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)v$. The paper also chooses a representative continuous in time. |
| **Norms and indices** | Vectors have the Euclidean norm. Sums of squared matrix entries give the squared Frobenius norm; norms of derivative maps are operator norms. Changing between them can change constants. Formal derivative arrays put the output component first, which transposes the paper's convention $(\nabla v)_{jk}=\partial_jv_k$ of (7.11) and the direction-first coefficients of (B.10). The paper's label $(\iota_1,\iota_2)$ gives the time and angle frequencies $(2\iota_2-\iota_1,\varkappa\iota_1)$. |
| **Recurrent profiles** | The smooth hypothesis requires (1.2), $S>0$ and $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$, with $R$ orthogonal and possibly orientation reversing. Pressure recurrence is not required. Hessian and pressure-gradient decay are explicit hypotheses beyond the bounds displayed in (1.3); Remark 1.2 supplies the Hessian bound and states no pressure-gradient bound. The weak conclusion has measurable representatives, explicit distributional identities, and no pressure or pointwise decay. |
| **Certificates and rows** | Data specify functions, arrays and proposed bounds; the certificate conditions require their identities and inequalities. The earlier box-and-ball estimates and the steady fractional variant are distinct from the extended classical certificate. The paper's row field equals $\sqrt{\tau}$ times the formal unit-normalized row, with the weight $\tau$ stored separately. At cell level the stored number is $c\tau$, with $c=3/50$ in the final system. |
| **Nonexistence conclusions** | For every $\nu>0$ there is a smooth divergence-free datum from which no global smooth unforced solution exists. On $\mathbb R^3$ the datum has compact support and the excluded solutions have kinetic energy bounded uniformly in $t\ge0$; on the torus the datum and the velocity of the excluded solutions are periodic in space. The datum may depend on $\nu$. The conclusions omit the finite blow-up time, the rates and the convergence to the profile of Theorem 1.1. The cell-system implications assume the full certificate conditions. |

**Conventions affecting meaning.** Natural-number subtraction stops at zero; some separate majorants use integer exponents. Division by zero, and the real square root of a negative argument, give zero. Each derivative operation gives zero where its own derivative fails; an iterated derivative differentiates the assigned first-derivative function, so there is no blanket zero rule for a Hessian. A nonintegrable ordinary integral or a nonsummable real, complex or vector series gives zero. Nonnegative integrals and series may be infinite, and conversion of infinity to a real number gives zero. A real supremum of an unbounded set gives zero. These assignments supply values outside the usual analytic hypotheses; they provide no regularity, finiteness or estimate. The glossary states the hypotheses needed for the analytic interpretation.

**Proofs.** The statement files give each theorem with its proof left open, so that an independent checker can compare them with the proofs supplied separately in the formalization. The formalization contains no certificate data, and the numerical verification of a certificate is not part of it (§1.5).

sec-2
rows.text: ### 2.1 The space $X$ and the notion of solution We write $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ for the space of smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free fields $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, and $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ for the space of the divergence-free fields $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\nabla u\in L^2$, with the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. For $t>0$ and a field $u$ in $L^p(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, $1\le p\le\infty$, let $$\begin{equation} e^{t\Delta}u=(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-|\cdot|^2/(4t)}*u,\tag{2.1} \end{equation}$$ and $e^{0\Delta}u=u$. For $\tau>0$ and a field $f$ that is the sum of a field in $L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and a field in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ let $$\begin{equation} e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P f=\mathcal F^{-1}\bigl[e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\,\mathbb P_\xi\hat f\bigr],\tag{2.2} \end{equation}$$ and for $u,v\in X$ let $$\begin{equation} K(\tau)(u,v)=-\tfrac12\,e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P\bigl[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u\bigr].\tag{2.3} \end{equation}$$ By Hölder’s inequality $(u\cdot\nabla)v\in L^{3/2}\subset L^1+L^2$, so that (2.3) is defined. The map $K(\tau)$ is bilinear and symmetric, it maps $X\times X$ into $X$ (Lemma 3.1), and $K(\tau)(u,u)=-e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)u]$. Let $a ### 2.2 Blow-up on $\mathbb R^3$ and on the torus On $\mathbb R^3$ we prove the following proposition. **Proposition 2.1.** Let $(W,q)$ be a profile, and let $u_1^*$ be the field (1.4) with $T=1$. Then there exist $\kappa\in(0,\tfrac14)$, constants $00$, and a finite-dimensional subspace $E$ of $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ with the following property. For every $w_0\in X$ with $\|w_0-W(0,\cdot)\|_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon_0$ there exist $\gamma\in E$ and a solution $u$ on $[0,1)$ with $u(0)=w_0+\gamma$ such that, for $0\le t<1$, $$\begin{equation} c\,(1-t)^{-\frac14}\le\|u(t)\|_{\dot H^1}\le C\,(1-t)^{-\frac14},\qquad \|u(t)-u_1^*(t)\|_{\dot H^1}\le C\,(1-t)^{\kappa-\frac14}.\tag{2.5} \end{equation}$$ Moreover, there is a field $w_0\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ with $\|w_0-W(0,\cdot)\|_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon_0$. The proof is in Sections 4 and 5; the field $w_0$ of the last assertion is $W(0,\cdot)$ cut off at a large radius (Lemma 5.1). On the torus we prove the following proposition, at a small blow-up time $T$. **Proposition 2.2.** Let $(W,q)$ be a profile. Then there exist $T\in(0,1]$, $\kappa\in(0,\tfrac14)$, constants $0 ### 2.3 Proof of Theorem 1.1 Proposition 2.1, for a field $w_0\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$, and Proposition 2.2 give mild solutions with smooth data, and it remains to show that these are smooth solutions of (1.1). We say that a mild solution $u$ is a smooth solution if the fields $u(t)$ are the values at time $t$ of a smooth solution with datum $u(0)$. **Lemma 2.3.** Let $0 $u$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$ with datum $u_0$, and it has finite energy. Since $\|u(t)\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^2}$, the bounds (2.5) are (1.6). On the torus, let $T$ and the solution on $[0,T)$ be given by Proposition 2.2; we denote this solution by $u_{\mathrm{per}}$. Its datum is smooth, so that, by Lemma 2.3, $u_{\mathrm{per}}$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,T)\times\mathbb T^3$, and (2.6) is (1.7). Finally, since $1-t\le1$ and $T-t\le1$, the bounds (1.6) and (1.7) hold with the smaller of the two exponents $\kappa$ and of the two constants $c$ and with the larger of the two constants $C$. $\square$ The same argument, for an arbitrary field $w_0\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ with $\|w_0-W(0,\cdot)\|_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon_0$, gives the stability in finite codimension stated after Theorem 1.1.

rows.label: sec-3
sec-4
sec-5
rows.text: In this section we prove Proposition 2.1. We keep the notation of Section 4. ### 5.1 The cutoff We cut the field $u^*(t)$ off at a radius $r$ through a vector potential, so that it remains divergence-free. We fix a function $\eta\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $0\le\eta\le1$, $\eta=1$ on $B_{1/2}$ and $\eta=0$ outside $B_1$, and for $r>0$ and $0\le t<1$ we let $$\begin{equation} A(t,x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x\,d\sigma,\qquad\bar u(t)=\operatorname{curl}\bigl(\eta(\cdot/r)\,A(t)\bigr).\tag{5.1} \end{equation}$$ We do not show the radius $r$ in the notation $\bar u$; it is fixed wherever the field is used. **Lemma 5.1.** There exists a constant $C$ such that for every $r>0$ the field $\bar u$ of (5.1) is smooth on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$, and for $0\le t<1$ the field $\bar u(t)$ belongs to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$, equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{r/2}$, vanishes outside $B_r$, and satisfies $$\begin{equation} \|\bar u(t)-u^*(t)\|_{\dot H^1}\le C\,r^{-1/2},\qquad\|\bar u(t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\,r^{1/2}.\tag{5.2} \end{equation}$$ *Proof.* In this proof the constants in $\lesssim$ do not depend on $r$ and $t$. Let $r>0$ and $0\le t<1$. The integrand in (5.1) is smooth in $(\sigma,t,x)$, so that $A$ and $\bar u$ are smooth on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Since $u^*(t)$ is divergence-free, $$ \operatorname{curl}_x[\sigma\,u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x]=\partial_\sigma[\sigma^2\,u^*(t,\sigma x)], $$ so that $\operatorname{curl}A(t)=u^*(t)$ and $$ \bar u(t)=\eta(\cdot/r)\,u^*(t)+r^{-1}(\nabla\eta)(\cdot/r)\times A(t). $$ Thus $\bar u(t)$, which is divergence-free as a curl, equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{r/2}$, where $\eta(\cdot/r)=1$, and vanishes outside $B_r$; in particular it belongs to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. By (4.1), in the form $|u^*(t,x)|\le C_W\,|x|^{-1}$ and $|\nabla u^*(t,x)|\le C_W\,|x|^{-2}$ at the points $\sigma x$, differentiation under the integral gives $$ |A(t,x)|\le C_W,\qquad|\nabla A(t,x)|\lesssim|x|^{-1}\qquad(x\ne0). $$ The field $\bar u(t)-u^*(t)=(\eta(\cdot/r)-1)\,u^*(t)+r^{-1}(\nabla\eta)(\cdot/r)\times A(t)$ vanishes on $B_{r/2}$ and equals $-u^*(t)$ outside $B_r$. By the product rule and these bounds, its gradient is at most a constant multiple of $r^{-2}$ for $\frac r2\le|x|\le r$, and at most $C_W\,|x|^{-2}$ for $|x|\ge r$. Hence $$ \|\bar u(t)-u^*(t)\|_{\dot H^1}^2\lesssim r^{-4}r^3+\int_{|x|\ge r}\frac{dx}{|x|^4}\lesssim r^{-1}. $$ By the same bounds $|\bar u(t,x)|\lesssim|x|^{-1}$ for $|x|\le r$, so that $\|\bar u(t)\|_{L^2}^2\lesssim\int_{|x|\le r}|x|^{-2}\,dx\lesssim r$. This is (5.2). $\square$ ### 5.2 Proof of Proposition 2.1 Let $\kappa$, $E$, $C_{\mathcal R}$ and $\mathcal R$ be given by Proposition 4.3, let $c_*$ be the constant of Lemma 4.2, and let $\varepsilon_1$ be the number of Lemma 4.8 on $X$ for this $\kappa$. We fix $\varepsilon_0>0$ with $$ C_{\mathcal R}^2\,\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon_1,\qquad4\,C_{\mathcal R}\,\varepsilon_0\le c_*. $$ Let $w_0\in X$ with $\|w_0-W(0,\cdot)\|_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon_0$, and let $\chi=w_0-u^*(0)$. Then $\|\chi\|_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon_0$, because $u^*(0)=W(0,\cdot)$ by (1.4). We apply Lemma 4.8 with $\mathcal X=X$ and $u^{\mathrm a}=u^*$, with the space $E$ and the inclusion $J$ of $E$ in $X$, and with the map $\mathcal R$ and the constant $C_{\mathcal R}$ of Proposition 4.3. Here $F^{\mathrm a}=0$, because $u^*$ is a solution (Proposition 4.1), and (4.22) is (4.8). By (4.20), $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le\|\chi\|_{\dot H^1}$, so that (4.23) holds, by the first condition on $\varepsilon_0$. The lemma gives $\gamma\in E$ and $v\in C_\kappa([0,1);X)$ such that $u=u^*+v$ is a solution on $[0,1)$ with $u(0)=u^*(0)+\chi+\gamma=w_0+\gamma$, and by (4.24) and the second condition on $\varepsilon_0$, $$ \|u(t)-u^*(t)\|_{\dot H^1}=\|v(t)\|_{\dot H^1}\le2\,C_{\mathcal R}\,\varepsilon_0(1-t)^{\kappa-\frac14}\le\tfrac12\,c_*(1-t)^{\kappa-\frac14}\qquad(0\le t<1). $$ This bound and (4.4) give (2.5), with $c=\frac12c_*$ and with a constant $C$ that does not depend on $w_0$. It remains to find a field $w_0$ of this kind in $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. By Lemma 5.1, whose constant does not depend on the radius, we can fix a radius $r$ so large that the field $\bar u(0)$ of (5.1), for this radius and $t=0$, satisfies $\|\bar u(0)-u^*(0)\|_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon_0$; this field belongs to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. $\square$

rows.text:
### A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3

*Proof of Lemma 3.3.* Since $K(\tau)$ is bilinear and continuous in $\tau$, the bound of (3.12) shows that the map $(\tau,\chi,\chi')\mapsto K(\tau)(\chi,\chi')$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal X$. Hence the integrand is continuous in $t'\in[a,t)$, with norm at most $C_K\,(t-t')^{-3/4}\max_{[a,b]}\|u\|_{\mathcal X}\,\max_{[a,b]}\|v\|_{\mathcal X}$, and it is integrable. After the substitution $\tau=t-t'$ the continuity of the integral in $t$ follows by dominated convergence. $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.4.* For $\beta>0$ we give the space of continuous maps $h:[a,b]\to\mathcal X$ the norm $\max_{a\leq t\leq b}e^{-\beta(t-a)}\|h(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$, which is equivalent to the supremum norm. By Lemma 3.3 the integral term of the equation of the lemma defines a linear map of this space into itself, and since $e^{-\beta(t-a)}=e^{-\beta(t-t')}e^{-\beta(t'-a)}$, the bound of (3.12) shows that the norm of this map is at most $$
 2C_K\max_{[a,b]}\|f\|_{\mathcal X}\int_0^\infty\tau^{-3/4}e^{-\beta\tau}\,d\tau,
$$ where the integral is a constant multiple of $\beta^{-1/4}$. For $\beta$ large the map is a contraction, which gives the lemma. $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.5.* We apply the bounded operator $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ to the identity for $u$ at time $m$. By (3.11) and the first identity of (3.12), $$
 e^{(t-m)\Delta}u(m)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))\,dt',
$$ and subtracting this from the identity at time $t$ gives (3.13). For the uniqueness, let $u$ and $v$ be two solutions on $[a,b]$ with $u(a)=v(a)$. Since $K$ is bilinear and symmetric, the difference $u-v$ satisfies the equation of Lemma 3.4 with $\frac12(u+v)$ in place of $f$ and with $g=0$, and hence $u=v$. $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.6.* Translating the time, we may assume that $a=0$. Let $E_2$ be the space of \[[46](#cite-ref46)\], the closure of the Schwartz functions on $\mathbb R^3$ in the norm $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}$. Since $\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^6}$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ is dense in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, this space contains $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, and by (3.1) $u$ is a continuous map from $[0,b]$ to $E_2$. Let $0<m<b$, and let $\varphi$ be a smooth, compactly supported field on $[0,m]\times\mathbb R^3$ that is divergence-free at each time. Since $u$ is continuous with <!-- source-page: 48 --> values in $L^6$, the hypothesis (3.14) for the fields $\psi=\varphi(t)$ and the product rule show that the function $t\mapsto\int u(t)\cdot\varphi(t)\,dx$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,m]$, with the derivative $$
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[u\cdot\bigl(\partial_t\varphi+\Delta\varphi\bigr)+\bigl(u\otimes u\bigr):\nabla\varphi\Bigr]\,dx.
$$ Integrating from 0 to $m$, we obtain the identity of the formulation (NSW) of \[[46](#cite-ref46)\] at the time $m$, with the datum $u(0)$; the fields $\varphi$ above are the test fields of that formulation. Thus $u$ is a solution of (NSW) on $(0,b)$, and by \[[46](#cite-ref46), Theorem 1\] there is a tempered distribution $v_0$ such that $$
 u(t)=e^{t\Delta}v_0-\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl(u(t')\otimes u(t')\bigr)\,dt'\qquad(0\leq t<b)
$$ in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^3)$. At $t=0$ this gives $v_0=u(0)$. The field $\operatorname{div}(u(t')\otimes u(t'))=(u(t')\cdot\nabla)u(t')$ belongs to $L^{3/2}$, so that the integrand is $-K(t-t')(u(t'),u(t'))$, by (2.2) and (2.3), and since the Schwartz fields are continuous linear functionals on $X$, by (3.1), the integral is that of (2.4). Thus (2.4) holds for $0\leq t<b$, and it holds at $t=b$ because both of its sides are continuous on $[0,b]$ with values in $X$ (Subsection 3.1 and Lemma 3.3). $\square$

*Proof of Lemma 3.7.* Let $L>0$ and $\tau>0$, let $f\in L^{3/2}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ have mean zero, and let $z=e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf$. Since $|\hat z(k)|\leq e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}L^{-3}\|f\|_{L^1(Q_L)}$, the field $z$ is smooth; it is real and divergence-free, and it has mean zero. Thus $z$ belongs to $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$, and so does the field $\Psi=-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}z$, whose Fourier coefficients are $4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)$. Since $\mathbb P_k$ is a real symmetric matrix and $\mathbb P_k\hat z(k)=\hat z(k)$, Parseval’s identity and (3.15) give $$
 \int_{Q_L}\Psi\cdot f\,dx=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)\cdot\overline{\hat f(k)}=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2|\hat z(k)|^2=\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2.
$$ Since $4\pi^2|k|^2\leq\tau^{-1}e^{4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}$, the norms of $\Psi$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and in $\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$ are at most $\tau^{-1/2}$ and $\tau^{-1}$ times $\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}$. By Hölder’s inequality and (3.18) for $\Psi$, $$
 \|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2\leq\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|\Psi\|_{L^2(Q_L)}^{1/2}\|\Psi\|_{L^6(Q_L)}^{1/2}\lesssim\tau^{-3/4}\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)},
$$ which gives (3.19). The identity $e^{t\Delta}e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf=e^{(t+\tau)\Delta}\mathbb Pf$ holds coefficient by coefficient, and with it the continuity in $\tau$ follows from that of the heat flow on $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$.

Let $u,v\in\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$. By Hölder’s inequality and (3.18), $$
 \|(u\cdot\nabla)v\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\leq\|u\|_{L^6(Q_L)}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(Q_L)}\lesssim\|u\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}\|v\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)},
$$ and the same holds with $u$ and $v$ exchanged. The field $(u\cdot\nabla)v=\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)$ has mean zero, and so has $(v\cdot\nabla)u$. The first part of the lemma, for $f=(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u$, therefore gives (3.20). $\square$

### A.2 Proof of Lemma 2.3

We deduce the lemma from the local theory in $H^1$, in the form given by Tao \[[84](#cite-ref84), Section 5\], which concerns solutions in a smaller class. An $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ in the sense of \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 31\], without force and with a divergence-free datum $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, is a divergence-free field $\tilde u\in L^\infty([0,b];H^1(\mathbb R^3))\cap L^2([0,b];H^2(\mathbb R^3))$ which satisfies the integral equation \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] with the datum $u_0$; its pressure $\tilde p$ is determined by $\tilde u(t)$ at each time $t$, through the formula \[[84](#cite-ref84), (9)\]. The periodic $H^1$ mild solutions of \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 29\] are defined in the same way on the torus. We show that such a solution with the datum $u(0)$ coincides with $u$ as long as it exists, and that its norm in $H^1$ remains bounded. By the alternative of \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] between existence and blow-up in $H^1$, it then exists on $[0,b]$ for every $b<T$, and $u$ has the smoothness that \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] proves in this class.

<!-- source-page: 49 -->

*Proof of Lemma 2.3.* Let $u$ be as in the first assertion, let $u_0=u(0)$ and $0<b<T$, and let $\tilde u$ be an $H^1$ mild solution on an interval $[0,b']$, $0<b'\leq b$, with datum $u_0$. By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i)\] it is a continuous map from $[0,b']$ to $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and since its values are divergence-free and $H^1(\mathbb R^3)\subset L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, it is a continuous map from $[0,b']$ to $X$. Since $\operatorname{div}\tilde u=0$, the integrand of \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] is $K(t-t')(\tilde u(t'),\tilde u(t'))$, so that the integral converges in $X$ as well, to the same field, and is continuous in $t$ with values in $X$, by Lemma 3.3. Both sides of the equation are therefore continuous in $t$ with values in $X$, so that it holds at every time. Thus $\tilde u$ is a mild solution on $[0,b']$, and $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$, by Lemma 3.5. Moreover, $u_0$ is a Schwartz field. Hence $\tilde u$ and $\tilde p$ are smooth on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$, and all their derivatives in $t$ and $x$ are bounded on $[0,b']$ with values in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(iv)\]. The formula \[[84](#cite-ref84), (10)\] is the integral form of (1.1), so that $(\tilde u,\tilde p)$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$ with datum $u_0$. By these bounds we may multiply (1.1) by $\tilde u$ and integrate by parts over $\mathbb R^3$, which gives $\frac d{dt}\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2=-2\|\nabla\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2\leq0$. Hence $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}$ and, since $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$, $$
 \|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}+\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\qquad(0\leq t\leq b').
$$ By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.8\], either there is an $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ with datum $u_0$, or there are $T_*\in(0,b]$ and a map $\tilde u$ from $[0,T_*)$ to $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ as $t\to T_*$, whose restriction to $[0,b']$ is an $H^1$ mild solution with datum $u_0$ for every $b'<T_*$. The second case does not occur, because the bound above holds on $[0,b']$ for every $b'<T_*$. Hence there is an $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ with datum $u_0$. As we have shown, it is the restriction of $u$ to $[0,b]$, it is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, and its norm in $L^2$ does not exceed that of $u_0$. Since $b<T$ is arbitrary, this proves the first assertion.

Now let $u$ be as in the second assertion, with the smooth datum $u_0$, and let $0<b<T$. The argument is the same, with the periodic $H^1$ mild solutions, whose velocity and pressure are periodic, with $K_{\mathbb T}$ in place of $K$, and with \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i) and (iv) and Corollary 5.2\] in place of \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i) and (iv) and Corollary 5.8\]. The datum has mean zero, as the theory on the torus requires \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1\]. A periodic $H^1$ mild solution with this datum is a continuous map into $H^1(\mathbb T^3)$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i)\] whose values are divergence-free and have mean zero \[[84](#cite-ref84), (39)\], and hence a continuous map into $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T^3)$, and Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5 apply in this space by Lemma 3.7. The second case of \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.2\] does not occur: in that case $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,T_*)$, and $\|u(t)\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}\lesssim\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T^3)}$ for $0\leq t<T_*$, by (3.16). Hence the restriction of $u$ to $[0,b]$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b]\times\mathbb T^3$, and since $b<T$ is arbitrary, this proves the second assertion. $\square$

sec-appendix-c
rows.text:
In this appendix we describe how the field from which the approximate profiles of the certificate of Subsection 1.1 are formed was found, and how further fields of this certificate were computed from it, and we show this field (Figures 1 to 4).

### C.1 The approximate profile

We write $\bar W$ for the computed approximate profile, as a field of the self-similar variables $(s,y)$, and $\bar S$ for its period in $s$. In the variable $\theta=s/\bar S$ it is a field of the form (B.6) of Subsection B.1, and the approximate profiles of the certificate are formed from it: in a ball about the origin they are the affine combinations of $\bar W$ with the fields of Subsection C.4, as in (B.9).

For this certificate the integer $\varkappa$ of (B.1) is $19$. The field $\bar W$ is a sum of harmonics (B.2) with this integer, and its terms satisfy the relations of Subsection B.1. Hence $\bar W$ is invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/19$ about the $y_3$ axis and under the rotation $R_*$ by $\pi$ about the $y_1$ axis, and an advance of $s$ by half the period rotates it by the angle $\pi/19$: $$
\bar W\bigl(s+\tfrac12\bar S,y\bigr)=R_{\pi/19}\,\bar W\bigl(s,R_{\pi/19}^{-1}\,y\bigr)\qquad(s\in\mathbb R,\ y\in\mathbb R^3).
$$ The harmonics $E_\iota$ with $\iota_2=0$ depend on $\theta$ and $\phi$ only through $\phi-2\pi\theta/19$, and those with $\iota_1=\iota_2$ only through $\phi+2\pi\theta/19$. Thus $\bar W$ contains two patterns that turn about the $y_3$ axis in opposite senses, each by the angle $2\pi/19$ in one period; the rotation $R_*$ exchanges them, <!-- source-page: 71 -->

![Figure 2](figures/figure-2.png)

*Figure 2.* The computed approximate profile $\bar W$ at $s=0$ in the meridional half plane, in the coordinates $r=(y_1^2+y_2^2)^{1/2}$ and $z=y_3$; angle brackets denote the mean over the angle $\phi$. Left: the azimuthal vorticity of the mean of $\bar W$, with level lines of its stream function. Middle: the azimuthal component of the mean. Right: the modulus of the harmonic $e^{19i\phi}$ of $\bar W$, on a logarithmic scale over four decades.

and every other harmonic is the product of a harmonic of the first pattern and of one of the second. The computed period is $\bar S\approx0.36$.

Figures 1, 2 and 3 show $\bar W$ at $s=0$. Its vorticity is concentrated in a column about the $y_3$ axis and, on either side of the plane $y_3=0$, in a layer that leaves the column and is divided into nineteen spiral arms (Figure 1). The mean of $\bar W$ over the angle $\phi$ is an axisymmetric field with swirl. Its azimuthal component has opposite signs on the two sides of the plane $y_3=0$, as the invariance under $R_*$ requires. Its azimuthal vorticity is concentrated in a thin layer, which runs along the plane at a distance from it and then turns into the direction of the axis, where it encloses the column, and the level lines of its stream function follow this layer (Figure 2, left and middle). The part of $\bar W$ that depends on $\phi$ is of the same order of magnitude as the mean. Its first harmonics, $e^{\pm19i\phi}$, are largest near the plane, about the outer end of the layer (Figure 2, right), and in a horizontal plane through the layer the vertical component of the vorticity forms nineteen spiral arms, which end in nineteen vortices (Figure 3). The mean over $\phi$ has period $\bar S/2$ in $s$, by the symmetry.

By the symmetry the norm $\|\nabla\bar W(s)\|_{L^2}$ has period $\bar S/2$, and in the computation it varies over a period by less than a thousandth of its value. Figure 4 shows how $\bar W$ is distributed in $|y|$. At the origin $\bar W$ vanishes, and its gradient there is a multiple, which depends on $s$, of the gradient of the field $(y_1,y_2,-2y_3)$ (Subsection B.1). The weighted suprema of $\bar W$ and of its first and second derivatives that are shown there are largest for $|y|$ between $10$ and $100$, and for larger $|y|$ they are nearly constant. The bounds (7.8) hold for $\bar W$ by its form; in the computation the constant that they require is of order $10^5$.

Thus the computed field decays like $|y|^{-1}$, and the radial phase of Subsection B.1 is made for such a far field. In $\bar W$ the radial phase is $$
f(\rho)=\frac{2\pi}{\bar S}\log\Bigl(1+\frac\rho{r_c^2}\Bigr),
$$ <!-- source-page: 72 -->

![Figure 3](figures/figure-3.png)

*Figure 3.* The vertical component $\omega_3$ of $\operatorname{curl}\bar W$ at $s=0$ in the plane $y_3=z_0=6.5$, which cuts the layer of vorticity above the plane $y_3=0$.

![Figure 4](figures/figure-4.png)

*Figure 4.* The decay of the computed approximate profile: the suprema over the angles and over a period of $(1+|y|)\,|\bar W|$ (solid), $(1+|y|)^2\,|\nabla\bar W|$ (dashed) and $(1+|y|)^3\,|\nabla^2\bar W|$ (dotted), as functions of $|y|$, on logarithmic scales.

with a radius $r_c>0$, and the term with the harmonic $E_\iota$ has $l=\iota_1-2\iota_2$, the opposite of the frequency of $E_\iota$ in $\theta$. The functions (B.5) are then $$
E_{\iota,l}(\theta,y)=e^{19i\iota_1\phi}\exp\Bigl(\frac{2\pi il}{\bar S}\Bigl[\log\Bigl(1+\frac{|y|^2}{r_c^2}\Bigr)-s\Bigr]\Bigr),\qquad s=\bar S\theta,
$$ <!-- source-page: 73 --> and for large $|y|$ the bracket is $2\log|y|-s$ up to a constant and a term of order $|y|^{-2}$. In the Eulerian variables of (1.4) we have $2\log|y|-s=2\log|x|-\log T$. Hence a field of the form (B.6) with these functions $E_{\iota,l}$, whose coefficients are asymptotic, for large $|y|$, to functions of the angles divided by $|y|$, corresponds through (1.4) to a field that has a limit as $t\to T$ at every $x\ne0$. Without the radial phase the coefficients of such a field would oscillate in $\log|y|$, with frequencies proportional to $l$, in every ring of the partition out to infinity.

### C.2 The discretization and Newton’s method

The computation uses the first two equations of (1.2) in the form $$\begin{equation}
\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W+\operatorname{curl}W\times W+\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W+\nabla H=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}W=0,\tag{C.1}
\end{equation}$$ where $H=q+\tfrac12|W|^2$. The unknown field is of the form (B.6), with $\varkappa=19$, with the radial phase above and with the exponents $h_0=2$ and $h=1$. Thus the unknowns are the coefficients of the piecewise polynomials $\mathsf A$, $\mathsf B$, $\mathsf S$ and $\mathsf T$ of (B.7) and (B.8) and the numbers $\gamma$, for finitely many harmonics, and the period. All the harmonics share one partition of the variables $(\sigma,\eta)$ of (B.3), into rings in the radius, the last of which reaches infinity, and into intervals of $\eta\ge0$; the half space $y_3<0$ is given by the relations of Subsection B.1 under $R_*$, which become conditions at $\eta=0$. On each rectangle of the partition each harmonic has degrees of its own in $\sigma$ and in $\eta$, or is absent, and the basis functions are joined across the rectangles to the orders that Subsection B.1 prescribes. With this form the divergence vanishes identically, the behaviour at the axis, at the origin and at infinity is that of the factors in (B.7) and (B.8), and the symmetries hold.

The equation is imposed in a weak form. We integrate (C.1) over a period and over $\mathbb R^3$ against fields of the same form on the same partition, with the exponent $h=3$ in place of $h=1$. These test fields are divergence-free, so that the term $\nabla H$ drops out, and there are as many of them as there are unknown coefficients. The products of harmonics in $\operatorname{curl}W\times W$ are formed on a grid in the two angles on which the harmonics depend, the integrals over each rectangle are computed by Gauss quadrature, and one further equation fixes the translation of the field in $s$; it is the equation that belongs to the unknown period. A computed field is judged by its residual: the left-hand side of (C.1) without $\nabla H$, computed pointwise from the representation on a set of harmonics larger than that of the field, after subtraction of a gradient fitted to it by least squares, and measured in the space $\mathcal H$ of Subsection 7.1. This number approximates the norm in $\mathcal H$ of the left-hand side of (C.1) for the best choice of $H$, and it steers the computation. The bounds (7.23) for the residuals (7.10) of a certificate are among the conditions that the rigorous computation verifies.

The discrete equations are solved by Newton’s method. The derivative of the equations with respect to the coefficients is the weak form of the linearized operator $$\begin{equation}
v\mapsto\partial_sv+\tfrac12v+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)v+\operatorname{curl}W\times v+\operatorname{curl}v\times W+\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}v\tag{C.2}
\end{equation}$$ at the current field $W$; its matrix is not formed, only applied to vectors. The linear system, bordered by the derivative with respect to the period and by the equation that fixes the translation in $s$, is solved by the flexible GMRES method. The preconditioner is a product of block solves, where a block is the linearized operator restricted to a group of neighbouring harmonics, in some blocks also to low degrees, and is factored by nested dissection over the rectangles of the partition. Newton’s iteration is stopped after at most five steps.

### C.3 Continuation and refinement

Newton’s method starts from a field that was reached by continuation, in other discretizations than that of Subsection C.2: finite differences, and <!-- source-page: 74 --> then spectral elements. The continuation takes place in the family of equations $$
\partial_sU+(1-g)\,U+g\,(y\cdot\nabla)U+(U\cdot\nabla)U+\nabla\pi=\nu\,\Delta U+F,\qquad\operatorname{div}U=0,
$$ with a scaling parameter $g$, a viscosity $\nu>0$ and a force $F$; the first two equations of (1.2) are the case $g=\tfrac12$, $\nu=1$, $F=0$. It begins with an axisymmetric steady state for $g$ near $0.502$ and a small force, computed from a field whose swirl changes sign across the plane $y_3=0$ and which is composed of a layer of fluid that flows inward along the plane, a column, and a jet along the axis. On this layer we superpose waves of finite amplitude, with azimuthal wave numbers from $14$ to $20$, whose dependence on time is a rigid rotation about the axis, and we bring the force to zero, together with a damping term that this step introduces. We then pass to the half space $y_3>0$, with one family of waves and with the azimuthal wave number as a real parameter. Without force the states so computed form two-parameter families, on which $g$ is a function of the parameters; on the first of these $g>\tfrac12$ everywhere, and the value $g=\tfrac12$ is reached on a second one. At $g=\tfrac12$ we superpose such a state and its image under $R_*$, which turns in the opposite sense, and we replace the condition at the plane $y_3=0$ by the exact one. Finally, through several refinements of the discretization, in which the viscosity takes the place of $g$ as an unknown, the wave number is brought to the integer $19$, and the result is projected onto a space of the form of Subsection C.2.

From this starting field the approximate profile is computed in nine successive discretizations of the form of Subsection C.2, each of which starts from the field of the one before, transferred to the new degrees. In the first three the viscosity is an unknown beside the period, and a normalization of the mean swirl is imposed: for the equations themselves, the solutions for different viscosities are dilations of one another, and the normalization selects one of them. The viscosity is then brought to one along this family. In the fourth discretization the viscosity is one and the period is an unknown; the period found there is $\bar S$, and it is kept in the five discretizations that follow. The ninth field is $\bar W$.

Between two discretizations the degrees are changed harmonic by harmonic and rectangle by rectangle, by one of two rules. In the first, the contribution of each harmonic on each rectangle to the residual, and the rate at which its coefficients decay with the degree, decide whether its degrees are raised or lowered, and harmonics are added on the rectangles on which the residual lies outside those that are present. In the second, the degrees are predicted from the decay of the coefficients alone, each weighted by estimates of the local rates of the terms of the equation. Far from the origin, where the radial phase has removed the oscillation of the spiral arms, the degrees in the radius are tied to the frequencies in $\log|y|$ that remain, and the degrees in $\eta$ are the same in all rings.

### C.4 Further fields of the certificate

The forcing fields $b_i$ and the fields $\Xi_i$ of the constraints (7.11) are computed from the equation linearized about a field of the sequence of Subsection C.3. On a space of perturbations coarser than that of the field, we solve the equation with the operator (C.2) for a given right-hand side, bordered as in Newton’s method by the derivative with respect to the period and by a condition that removes the translation in $s$. Perturbations are measured in a norm of the form of (7.14) with a constant weight $w>0$, and right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$. A block Lanczos iteration gives the right-hand sides for which the solution is largest relative to the right-hand side, with their solutions. Finitely many of these pairs are kept, and to them is added the pair that accounts for the translations in time: the left null vector of the bordered system and the derivative of the field in $s$. For each pair, the forcing field $b_i$ is obtained from the right-hand side, and the constraint from the solution $v_i$, <!-- source-page: 75 --> through the field $w\,v_i-\Delta v_i$: for a divergence-free field $v$, $$
\bigl\langle\nabla v,\nabla(w\,v_i-\Delta v_i)\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\Delta v,\Delta v_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}+w\,\langle\nabla v,\nabla v_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
$$ is the inner product of $v$ and $v_i$ that belongs to this norm. Both fields are cut off in the radius and smoothed, in such a way that they remain divergence-free and keep the symmetries. The fields $\Phi_i$ and $\Xi_i$ of Subsection B.1 are then produced on a mesh of cells of the meridian plane, obtained by repeated division of a cell into four: $\Phi_i$ is, up to a normalization, $r$ times a spline fitted by least squares, whose coefficients are integer multiples of a power of $2$, and $\Xi_i$ is a polynomial on each cell, with rounded coefficients, which approximates $\nabla\Phi_i$. This is why $\Xi_i$ is not a gradient, and why Subsection B.1 has the number $c_\Xi$.

The fields $W^i$ of (B.9), $1\le i\le n$, with the vectors $\beta^i$ and the numbers $\varsigma_i$ of Subsection B.1, are computed approximate solutions of the linearized equation in which a combination of the forcing fields and a change of the period are unknowns and the values of the constraints are prescribed: with the field $F^{(i)}$ of (B.57), they solve approximately the equation $F^{(i)}\simeq0$. A change of the period changes the radial phase, which is tied to the period. In these fields the change is made only outside a ball, which is the origin of the function $f_*$ of (B.9), so that inside the ball the approximate profiles are affine in the parameter. The adjoint fields $\psi_j$ are computed approximate solutions of the adjoint of the linearized equation whose right-hand sides are combinations of the fields that represent the constraints, as (7.33) requires, with prescribed pairings with the forcing fields, which (7.35) compares with the columns of the matrix $V$; they are sought with the exponent $h=3$.

The weights $\lambda_p$ and $\mu_p$ of the multiplier (B.14) act on the harmonics outside the range $|\iota_2|\le j_*$, $|\iota_2-\iota_1|\le j_*$. In the computation the rates of rotation $\nu_p$ are, up to the sign, the angular velocity $2\pi/(19\,\bar S)$ of the two patterns of Subsection C.1. In the frame that turns with the first pattern the frequency (B.15) of the harmonic $\iota$ is $4\pi\iota_2/\bar S$, and in the frame that turns with the second it is $-4\pi(\iota_1-\iota_2)/\bar S$: outside the range each harmonic has, in one of the two frames, a frequency of modulus larger than $4\pi j_*/\bar S$. The multiplier turns this frequency into positive terms, proportional to $\lambda_p\,|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ and to $\mu_p\,|\Omega_p(\iota)|$, in the coefficients of (B.16). Among the errors that these terms have to absorb is the transport by $W^{\mathrm r}+\tfrac12y-\nu_p\,\mathbf e_z\times y$, the velocity relative to this frame; if this error alone is taken into account, without the derivatives of the weight, the best weight at a point is proportional to the frequency divided by the square of this speed. The weights are splines in the variables (B.3), and their coefficients are found by a numerical optimization, which maximizes the smallest, over the cells and over the classes of harmonics, of the differences between the two sides of the inequalities in which the weights enter, each suitably normalized.

rows.label: sec-finite-time-blow-up-for-the-navier-stokes-equations
rows.text:
• Levent Alpöge
  • Tristan Buckmaster
We prove that there exist smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free initial data on $\mathbb R^3$, and smooth divergence-free initial data on the torus $\mathbb T^3$, for which the solutions of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations without force blow up in finite time. This disproves the statements (A) and (B) of the Millennium Prize problem as formulated by Fefferman, and hence proves the statements (C) and (D). These solutions converge in self-similar variables to a backward discretely self-similar solution and blow up at its rate, which is $(T-t)^{-1/4}$ in $\dot H^1$. The discretely self-similar solution is obtained from a certificate: an approximate solution that satisfies explicit inequalities. The certificate will be released soon; its hash is `3f7a335b84b6c7631742cacc5343dfcd11cf72f5221ff79b2b9268790b4b22c5`.

# From a recurrent profile to unforced Navier–Stokes blow-up

**Navier–Stokes pages:** [the paper](../navier-stokes-paper/paper.pdf) · [index by number](../navier-stokes-index/paper.md) · **specialist digest** · [full account, part I](../navier-stokes-part-1/paper.md) · [part II](../navier-stokes-part-2/paper.md) · [part III](../navier-stokes-appendix-b/paper.md) · [what the Lean states](paper.md) · [statement files](../navier-stokes-statement-files/paper.md) · [proof routes](../navier-stokes-routes/paper.md) · [proof routes in detail](../navier-stokes-route-details/paper.md) · [library guide](../navier-stokes-library-01/paper.md) · [cell layer guide](../navier-stokes-cell-guide/paper.md) · [cell reference](../navier-stokes-cell-reference/paper.md) · [cell layer and Appendix B](cell-layer-fidelity.md) · [certificate checker](certificate-checker.md)

**A specialist digest of the paper by Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster**  
20 November 2026 · Lean at commit [`ad53419`](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/tree/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546)

rows.label: sec-1-the-conditional-theorem-and-its-proof
rows.text: ### 1.1 The profile hypothesis We work first with viscosity one: $$ \partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0, \qquad \operatorname{div}u=0. \tag{1.1} $$ **Definition 1.1 (recurrent similarity profile; paper (1.2)–(1.3), p. 2).** A profile consists of smooth fields $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, a number $S>0$, and an orthogonal map $R:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, satisfying $$ \partial_sW+\frac12W+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W +(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0, \qquad \operatorname{div}W=0, \tag{1.2} $$ $$ W(s+S,y)=R\,W(s,R^{-1}y),\qquad W\not\equiv0, \tag{1.3} $$ and, for one finite constant independent of $s$ and $y$, $$ |W(s,y)|\le C_W(1+|y|)^{-1},\qquad |\nabla W(s,y)|\le C_W(1+|y|)^{-2}. \tag{1.4} $$ An orthogonal map here may reverse orientation. Define its action on fields by $\rho_Rf(y)=R f(R^{-1}y)$. The gradient norm and the Navier–Stokes equation are invariant under this action. The formal profile predicate records the same equation and recurrence, together with bounds for second spatial derivatives of the velocity and the first spatial derivative of the pressure. The extra bounds are $$ |\nabla^2W(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3},\qquad |\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}. \tag{1.5} $$ The spatial regularity argument and the pressure reconstruction in Appendix A explain their derivation from the profile hypothesis. This is an analytic bridge supplied in the exposition. The linked formal predicate itself assumes those bounds. The proof of pressure decay also removes the harmonic ambiguity in reconstructing pressure; spatial derivative estimates for $W$ alone do not justify an unsupported estimate for $\partial_sW$. For a prospective blow-up time $T>0$, put $$ s=\log\frac{T}{T-t},\qquad y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{T-t}},\qquad u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,y), \quad p_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1}q(s,y). \tag{1.6} $$ Section 3 verifies the equation, the recurrence and the norm identities in these variables. The time variable $s$ is normalised so that $s=0$ at $t=0$. This normalisation matters when comparing the solution on the unit torus with the original profile. ### 1.2 Theorem A: the full construction **Theorem A (conditional finite-time blow-up; paper Theorem 1.1, p. 3).** Assume Definition 1.1. There are a number $\kappa\in(0,1/4)$ and positive constants $c,C$ with the following properties. There is a smooth compactly supported divergence-free datum $u_0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ whose viscosity-one solution has smooth velocity and pressure on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$, satisfies $\|u(t)\|_2\le\|u_0\|_2$, and obeys $$ c(1-t)^{-1/4}\le\|\nabla u(t)\|_2\le C(1-t)^{-1/4}, \qquad \|\nabla(u(t)-u_1^*(t))\|_2\le C(1-t)^{\kappa-1/4}. \tag{A-space} $$ There are a time $T\in(0,1]$, a smooth divergence-free datum on the unit torus, and a solution $u_{\mathrm{per}}$ with smooth periodic velocity and pressure on $[0,T)\times\mathbb T^3$ such that $$ c(T-t)^{-1/4}\le\|u_{\mathrm{per}}(t)\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)} \le C(T-t)^{-1/4}, \tag{A-torus-rate} $$ $$ \|u_{\mathrm{per}}(t)-u_T^*(t)\|_{H^1(B_{1/16})} \le C(T-t)^{\kappa-1/4}. \tag{A-torus-profile} $$ The constants can be enlarged, and $\kappa$ decreased, to use common values in these assertions. On whole space there are also a fixed finite-dimensional subspace $E\subset C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ and a fixed $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that every $w_0\in X$ with $\|w_0-W(0)\|_X\le\varepsilon_0$ admits some $\gamma\in E$ for which a mild solution with datum $w_0+\gamma$ satisfies the estimates in (A-space). If $w_0$ is smooth and compactly supported, the resulting solution has the stated smoothness and finite-energy bound. At least one such compactly supported $w_0$ exists. The fixed space $E$ is chosen before the nearby datum $w_0$; only the correction $\gamma$ depends on that datum. This quantifier order is the content of the finite-codimension assertion. It does not assert an open set of blowing-up data, and it does not identify a smooth manifold of such data. **Proof, organised by dependency.** Section 2 establishes the space, heat estimates, the mild equation and the compactness of the positive-time linearised interaction. Section 3 places $u_1^*$ in that framework and proves a strictly positive lower bound for its rescaled norm. Section 4 turns those facts into a finite-dimensional spectral obstruction. Section 5 selects compactly supported corrections which satisfy the boundary condition at infinite rescaled time. Section 6 solves the nonlinear correction equation, proves the fixed-$E$ assertion and constructs the compact initial approximation. Section 7 identifies the resulting mild solution with the classical solution on every compact time interval, proves its uniform energy bound and derives the two-sided rate. Sections 8 and 9 construct the exact unforced periodic solution and rescale it to the unit torus. These steps prove all clauses of Theorem A. The auxiliary analytic results used at those steps are stated and proved or supplied with exact external hypotheses in Appendix A. $\square$ The norm estimates have different roles. The upper bounds control the perturbation space. The positive lower bounds prove growth of the solution itself. The convergence bounds say that the error is smaller than the background by a factor tending to zero. In whole-space similarity variables $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}U(s,y)$ they imply $$ \|\nabla(U(s)-W(s))\|_2\le C e^{-\kappa s}. \tag{1.7} $$ For the periodic solution the comparison is local in physical coordinates. Its comparison domain in similarity coordinates is $B_{(16\sqrt{T-t})^{-1}}$. Every fixed similarity ball eventually lies in that domain. The estimate does not assert convergence in a whole-space norm of a periodically repeated field. ### 1.3 What the linked formal endpoints state The library proves that its smooth-profile premise implies the two formal breakdown predicates. On whole space the formal conclusion says: for every viscosity $\nu>0$, some smooth compactly supported divergence-free datum has no global smooth solution whose kinetic energy stays bounded. On the torus it says: for every $\nu>0$, some smooth periodic divergence-free datum has no global smooth solution with periodic velocity, with no periodicity hypothesis imposed on its pressure. These are the predicates `Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace` and `Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus`. Those endpoints do not display all the rates, profile comparisons and simultaneous choices in Theorem A. Intermediate declarations carry additional construction information, and Sections 4–9 describe it where it is used. The correspondence records therefore distinguish a matching local statement from an abstract result used in its proof, or an endpoint with a different conclusion. The paper's continuous weighted right inverse and the formal proof's bounded sequences of short pieces also receive separate descriptions. The whole-space endpoint follows from the constructed solution and finite-energy uniqueness; the periodic endpoint also uses a moving change of frame to handle a pressure with an affine part. The change $$ u^{(\nu)}(t,x)=\nu u(\nu t,x),\qquad p^{(\nu)}(t,x)=\nu^2p(\nu t,x) \tag{1.8} $$ carries a viscosity-one solution to viscosity $\nu$. Sections 7 and 9 give the precise exclusions and the pressure normalisation needed for them.

rows.label: sec-1-the-input-orbit-and-the-actual-conclusion
rows.text:
The analytic half of the argument starts with a profile; it does not construct one. Let $S>0$, $R\in O(3)$ and let $(W,q)$ be a smooth, nonzero solution on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ of

$$
\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0,
\qquad \nabla\cdot W=0,
$$

with $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ and uniform bounds $|W|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-1}$, $|\nabla W|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-2}$. For a chosen terminal time $T$, define

$$
s=\log\frac{T}{T-t},\qquad y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{T-t}},\qquad
u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,y).
$$

The transformed pressure is $(T-t)^{-1}q(s,y)$. Substitution gives the unforced viscosity-one Navier–Stokes equations. With $\lambda=e^{-S}$, one similarity period corresponds to $t\mapsto T-\lambda(T-t)$ and spatial contraction by $\sqrt\lambda$.

The profile is recurrent in logarithmic time, rather than stationary. This distinction is necessary: a stationary profile in the stated $L^6$ class is excluded by the classical nonexistence theory recalled in the paper. The $1/|y|$ upper bound permits an infinite-energy tail and does not supply strong $L^3$ control; it does not, by itself, prove that either norm diverges. What is supplied is membership in the space used below.

Theorem 1.1 asserts considerably more than existence of this possibly infinite-energy solution. It constructs $u_0\in C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and a smooth, uniformly finite-energy solution on $[0,1)$ for which, for some $0<\kappa<1/4$,

$$
c(1-t)^{-1/4}\le\|\nabla u(t)\|_2\le C(1-t)^{-1/4},
\qquad
\|\nabla(u-u_1^*)(t)\|_2\le C(1-t)^{\kappa-1/4}.
$$

It also constructs smooth data on the unit torus and a solution blowing up at some $T\in(0,1]$, with the same two-sided $H^1$ rate and the local estimate

$$
\|u_{\mathrm{per}}(t)-u_T^*(t)\|_{H^1(B_{1/16})}
\le C(T-t)^{\kappa-1/4}.
$$

These error bounds allow the physical error to grow. Multiplication by $(T-t)^{1/4}$ shows that its size relative to the profile tends to zero. In similarity variables the convergence is exponential, at rate $e^{-\kappa s}$. The torus comparison is local in physical space; that fixed physical ball expands to exhaust $\mathbb R^3$ in similarity coordinates.

**Paper:** §1.1, (1.2)–(1.7), pp. 2–3. **Formal anchor:** `Breakdown.profileOrbit_holds`, [`Profile/Orbit.lean:39–41`](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/blob/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean/Breakdown/Profile/Orbit.lean#L39-L41), constructs the abstract recurrent orbit from the formal smooth-profile premise. The public conclusions `Breakdown.breakdown_on_space` and `Breakdown.breakdown_on_torus` in [`Solution.lean`](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/blob/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean/Solution.lean) exclude global smooth solutions in specified classes: uniformly finite-energy solutions on the whole space, and solutions with periodic velocity on the torus. They do not themselves state the displayed quantitative bundle. The formal profile premise writes additional second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay assumptions. Remark 1.2 supplies the higher spatial derivative bound. A pressure-normalization argument gives the gradient bound: the difference from the Riesz-transform pressure is harmonic, and testing in time makes it decay at infinity without assuming a bound on the time derivative. This is an analytic bridge, not yet a Lean declaration.

rows.label: sec-1-the-result-and-its-notation
rows.text:
### 1.1 Theorem II.1: the full conclusion of Theorem 7.1

**Theorem II.1.** Suppose a certificate satisfies the conditions set out in §2 below. There exist a single parameter $\alpha_*\in K$, a smooth velocity $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, and a smooth pressure $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, with $S=S(\alpha_*)>0$, such that

$$
\partial_sW+\frac12W+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W
 +(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0,
\qquad \nabla\cdot W=0,
\qquad W(s+S,y)=W(s,y).
$$

The velocity is nonzero and, for one finite constant $C$, satisfies

$$
|W(s,y)|\le \frac{C}{1+|y|},
\qquad |\nabla W(s,y)|\le \frac{C}{(1+|y|)^2}.
$$

Define the correction using that same parameter and that same velocity:

$$
v_*(\theta,y)=W(S\theta,y)-W^a_{\alpha_*}(\theta,y).
$$

Then $v_*\in D_S^\Gamma$, and all of the following hold together:

$$
\|v_*\|_w^2+\omega^2|\beta^a(\alpha_*)|^2\le4\varepsilon^2,
\qquad
\|\nabla v_*(\theta)\|_2\le M\quad\text{for every }\theta\in\mathbb R,
\qquad
\ell(v_*)=\bar\ell(\alpha_*).
\tag{II.1}
$$

For every $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$, the same velocity satisfies

$$
W(s+S\theta_0,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y)
\quad\text{for every }(s,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3.
\tag{II.2}
$$

These are the complete velocity, correction and symmetry conclusions of the paper's Theorem 7.1, including the multiplier term in (7.38). Spatial second derivatives of the correction are weak derivatives. The approximate field is only required to have the regularity stated in the certificate, so subtracting it from a smooth field does not make its Hessian classical. The norm in (II.1) is finite, and its gradient integrand uses the Frobenius matrix norm.

The period is the specified $S(\alpha_*)$; it need not be the least period. The theorem prescribes velocity symmetries. No choice of pressure gauge is part of its quantitative conclusion. The proof is completed in §12. [P, Theorem 7.1 and (7.38)–(7.39), p.35.]

### 1.2 Dictionary

In the table, $d$ has type `Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData`. Its field names are qualified by that type. This convention makes the distinction between stored data and proved properties visible. The formal representations of $X$, $H$ and the graph domains are related by physical-reading lemmas; they are not literal synonyms for the paper's spaces.

| Symbol | Meaning in this account | Lean representation or interface |
|---|---|---|
| $s,\theta=s/S$ | Similarity time and period-one time | Real time; `Breakdown.Cert.TimeCircle` represents $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ |
| $y$ | Spatial similarity variable in $\mathbb R^3$ | `Breakdown.Space` |
| $X$ | Solenoidal homogeneous $H^1$, realised by $L^6$ fields | `Breakdown.Freq.X` encodes the homogeneous derivative symbol; physical readings recover the velocity |
| $H$ | $L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$ of periodic vector fields | `Breakdown.periodNorm`; `Breakdown.Cert.HH` represents the projected Fourier forcing |
| $P$ | Leray projection, at each time | `Breakdown.Cert.solProj`, `Breakdown.Cert.physToHH` |
| $T_S$ | $S^{-1}\partial_\theta+\frac12+\frac12y\cdot\nabla-\Delta$ | Free inverse: `Breakdown.Cert.freeInv`; physical equation: `Breakdown.IsPerturbation` and `Breakdown.IsRightSide` |
| $D_S^\Gamma$ | Periodic invariant graph domain of $T_S$ with $\Delta v\in H$ | `Breakdown.IsPerturbation`; its stored transport field is $T_Sv+\Delta v$ |
| $\Gamma$ | Prescribed orthogonal spatial actions with time shifts | `d.symmetries`, using `Breakdown.Symmetry` |
| $m\in\{1,2\}$ | Period reduction of scalar enstrophy | `d.twist` |
| $\alpha\in K\subset\mathbb R^n$ | Parameter and its box-times-ball domain | `Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params`; the Lean dimension is named $k$ |
| $S(\alpha),S_{\max}$ | Period and upper bound | `d.period`, `d.periodMax` |
| $W^a_\alpha,W^r_\alpha$ | Approximate field and reference field | `d.profile`, `d.model` |
| $F^a_\alpha$ | Chosen residual representative modulo gradients | `Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect` |
| $\beta^a(\alpha),b_i,b_*$ | Approximate force coefficients, directions and their bound | `d.multiplier`, `d.actuator`, `d.actuatorBound` |
| $\beta$ | Correction force coefficients | The finite vector in the held solution; normalised internally by $\omega$ |
| $\Xi_i,\ell_i(v)$ | Pin field and its gradient pairing | `d.pin`, `Breakdown.pinValue` |
| $\bar\ell(\alpha)$ | Required pin values for the correction | `Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.targetGap`; `d.target` stores full-profile pins |
| $w,w_*,w^{\max},\omega$ | Spatial weight, lower and upper bounds, multiplier weight | `d.weightFn`, `d.weight`, `d.weightMax`, `d.multiplierWeight` |
| $\lVert v\rVert_w^2, \lvert u\rvert_w^2$ | Period-integrated and single-slice derivative energies | `Breakdown.weightedEnergy`, `Breakdown.stationaryEnergy` |
| $\lvert\nabla v\rvert_{\rm F}^2$ | Sum of squares of all gradient entries | `Breakdown.matSq`; not the squared operator norm |
| $[F],c_0$ | Finite-row seminorm and its $H$ bound | `Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.rows`, `d.rowBound` |
| $c_1,c_2,c_L$ | Reference forcing constant, pin constant, zero-pin inverse constant | `d.coerciveL2`, `d.coercivePin`, `d.coerciveTotal` |
| $c_r,\vartheta$ | Reference error and absorbable loss | `d.gapSize`, `Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.transferLoss` |
| $c_3$ | Lower-bound constant for the frozen quadratic form | `d.formBound`; obtained from `d.modelFormBound` and `d.formShift` |
| $\delta(\alpha),\delta_0(\alpha),\delta_{\max}$ | Residual norm, row and uniform bounds | `d.defectBound`, `d.defectRowBound`, `d.defectMax` |
| $\varepsilon,M,\rho=2\varepsilon$ | Half the joint radius, gradient supremum radius, joint radius | `d.sizeBound`, `d.supBound`; the factor two is explicit |
| $c_w$ | $(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$ | `Breakdown.supBoundFactor` |
| $J,\rho_j,\rho_*,d_j$ | Box coordinates, their radii, ball radius and nonzero scales | `d.adjointSet`, `d.radius`, `d.stiffRadius`, `d.scale` |
| $V_j$ | Column $j$ of an invertible matrix $V$ | `d.frame`; the update uses its transpose |
| $\psi_{\alpha,j},Y(\alpha)$ | Approximate adjoints and pin coupling | `d.adjoint`, `d.coupling` |
| $a_j,\widetilde a_j,o_j$ | Adjoint linear, quadratic and affine errors | `d.adjointDefect`, `d.adjointQuad`, `d.adjointOffset` |
| $a_*,o_*$ | Joint bound and affine offset on the remaining coordinates | `d.stiffNorm`, `d.stiffOffset` |
| $\mathcal E$ | Complete spatial derivative space used before solving the time equation | `Breakdown.Cert.XX`, built from `Breakdown.Cert.XBar` |
| $A(v,\beta),B(v)$ | Joint weighted norm and essential gradient supremum | `Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ` after normalisation; `Breakdown.Cert.supGrad` |

The pin translation is $\bar\ell_i(\alpha)=d.\mathrm{target}(\alpha)_i-\ell_i(W^a_\alpha)$. Thus a statement about the correction's pin and a statement about the full field's pin express the same constraint only after this subtraction. Likewise, the stored transport field in `IsPerturbation` includes the dilation and time derivative before subtracting the Laplacian. These two translations will be used explicitly.

### 1.3 What the formal endpoints retain

The authors' declaration `Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_proved` proves that an extended certificate yields an existential weak periodic profile. Its conclusion does not retain the chosen parameter, the correction, or the full inequality (II.1). The argument inside the library supplies much of that information before the final existential packaging.

Our [Theorem 7.1 wrapper](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/tree/main/lean-wrappers/navier-stokes-theorem71) keeps those witnesses through regularity and states (II.1) for the actual smooth-profile difference. It compiles against the authors' package, with a small patch that adds keeping variants of three existential lemmas, and `Breakdown.theorem71_extended` and `Breakdown.theorem71_cell` use only the standard axioms ([run 44844164476](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/actions/runs/44844164476)). Its declarations are not shown beside this account, which links only the authors' Lean. The mathematical transport proof in §12 is written out independently.

rows.label: sec-10-the-parameter-argument-removes-the-force-exactly
rows.text:
The parameter domain is a product of a box and a weighted ball:

$$
K=\left\{\alpha:|\alpha_j|\le\rho_j\ (j\in J),\
\sum_{j\notin J}d_j^2\alpha_j^2\le\rho_*^2\right\}.
$$

With $V_j$ the columns of an invertible matrix and each $d_j\ne0$, define

$$
\Phi=\beta^a(\alpha)+\beta,\qquad
\alpha'_j=\alpha_j-d_j^{-1}V_j\cdot\Phi.
$$

The decisive assertion is that the raw update satisfies $\alpha'\in K$. An outward update at a boundary point can be fixed by nearest-point projection while $\Phi\ne0$.

For $j\in J$, pair the equation with an approximate adjoint $\psi_{\alpha,j}$. The adjoint-defect condition at $v=0$ forces this field to annihilate gradients, which makes pairing an equation modulo gradients legitimate. The adjoint-defect, nonlinear and affine-offset estimates give

$$
|V_j\cdot\Phi-d_j\alpha_j|
\le\widetilde a_j(2\varepsilon)^2
+2\varepsilon\sqrt{a_j^2+
\frac{|\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_H-V_j|^2}{\omega^2}}
+o_j
\le |d_j|\rho_j.
$$

The middle square root combines the velocity and multiplier errors using their **joint** weighted norm. For the remaining coordinates the bound is $2\varepsilon a_*/\omega+o_*\le\rho_*$. These are precisely the two membership conditions for the raw update. In the paper, the Schauder map used its projection; membership now removes the projection. In Lean, the continuous raw update is already a self-map of $K$, so a compact-convex fixed-point theorem applies. At a fixed point, $V^\mathsf T\Phi=0$, hence $\Phi=0$. Non-strict inclusions suffice: the fixed point may lie on the boundary, and $K$ may have empty interior.

The resulting profile $\mathcal W=W^a_\alpha+v$ is nonzero because (7.28) requires

$$
4\varepsilon^2<w_*\|\nabla W^a_\alpha\|_H^2.
$$

If $\mathcal W=0$, the correction bound would give the reverse inequality. Thus neither residual smallness nor a Newton heuristic substitutes for the force-zero and nonzero-profile steps.

**Paper:** (7.29)–(7.37), Proposition 7.10 and §7.9, pp.33–35 and 42–45. **Lean:** `Breakdown.Cert.extendedAdjointEnclosureHolds_of`, `extendedStiffEnclosureHolds`, `extendedExistsZeroHeldHolds_of`, `extendedHeldWeakEquationHolds_of` and `extendedHeldNonzeroHolds_of`; `Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of` is at [`Breakdown/Held/TestSetZero.lean:92`](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/blob/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean/Breakdown/Held/TestSetZero.lean#L92). Its compact-convex input is supplied by `convexCompactFixedPoint` and the proved `Breakdown.exists_fixedPoint_box`.

rows.label: sec-10-the-selected-weak-profile
rows.text: ### 10.1 Proposition II.16: cancellation and nontriviality **Proposition II.16.** For the selected $\alpha_*$, put $S=S(\alpha_*)$, $v=v_{\alpha_*}$ and $\mathcal W=W^a_{\alpha_*}+v$. Then $\mathcal W$ is a nonzero continuous period-one curve in $X$, and $$ T_S\mathcal W+N(\mathcal W)\simeq0. \tag{II.50} $$ Every term in this distributional equation is represented by a locally integrable function. To prove the equation, add the approximate relation (II.4) to the correction equation (II.5). The quadratic expansion contributes the two cross terms whose sum is $C_\alpha v$, together with the pure correction term $N(v)$. The residuals cancel, and the total force coefficients cancel by (II.49). This gives (II.50). The correction is continuous in $X$ by Lemma II.3. For the approximate profile, continuity of the gradient and (II.3) permit dominated convergence in $L^2_y$: the square is bounded by a constant times $(1+|y|)^{-4}$, integrable in dimension three. Its velocities are likewise continuous in $L^6$, using $(1+|y|)^{-6}$. Thus the sum is a continuous periodic $X$ curve. For local integrability of the correction's time derivative, solve the graph identity for it: $$ S^{-1}\partial_\theta v =T_Sv+\Delta v-\frac12v-\frac12y\cdot\nabla v. $$ The first two fields are in $H$. On bounded spatial sets the last two are locally square integrable, by $v\in L^2_\theta L^6_y$ and the gradient bound. Thus the time derivative is locally square integrable. The approximate field has the required local derivatives by hypothesis, and the quadratic and cross terms have the bounds from §4. This verifies all local-integrability requirements without separating the time and dilation terms globally. If $\mathcal W$ vanished, then $\nabla v=-\nabla W^a_{\alpha_*}$, so $$ w_*\|\nabla W^a_{\alpha_*}\|_H^2 =w_*\|\nabla v\|_H^2 \le\|v\|_w^2\le A(v,\beta)^2\le4\varepsilon^2. $$ This contradicts (II.14). The strict profile-separation inequality, rather than residual smallness alone, supplies nontriviality. The formal steps are `Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldWeakEquationHolds_of` and `Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldNonzeroHolds_of`. [P, proof of Theorem 7.1, pp.44–45.]

rows.label: sec-11-regularity-is-recovered-from-the-constructed-solution
rows.text:
The corrected field is continuous into $X$, periodic, and solves the similarity equation modulo gradients. The next estimates describe the paper's proof of Proposition 7.11; the formal proof uses a different smoothing and decay argument, identified below. The proposition assumes the constructed profile and, after returning to physical variables, already has

$$
u\in C((-\infty,1);L^6),
\qquad
\sup_{t<1}(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_6<\infty.
$$

Lemma 3.6 identifies this weak solution with its mild evolution. Two heat/Oseen estimates then give

$$
\|u(t)\|_{12}\lesssim(1-t)^{-3/8},
\qquad
\|u(t)\|_\infty\lesssim(1-t)^{-1/2}.
$$

The nonlinear kernels have time singularities $(t-\tau)^{-7/8}$ and $(t-\tau)^{-3/4}$, respectively, both integrable. The solution is consequently bounded on every compact interval before time 1. Bounded-mild regularity gives a smooth velocity; the smooth residual is curl-free, so a smooth pressure can be recovered. Ordinary discrete self-similarity with factor $e^{S/2}$ then permits the Chae–Wolf decay theorem at $p=6$:

$$
|u(t,x)|\lesssim\frac1{\sqrt{1-t}+|x|}.
$$

Scaling back gives the required profile decay, and interior estimates give derivative decay. This route never requires finite kinetic energy of the profile. Recovering the full same-witness conclusion also requires identifying the smooth representative with the originally selected correction at every time. Equality in $X$ then preserves the correction norms and pins; continuity upgrades each almost-everywhere symmetry to pointwise symmetry.

With its analytic inputs supplied, the formal weak-profile bridge gives a continuous mild orbit. For each chosen mild orbit, the formal smoothing statement returns smooth velocity and pressure together with equality to that orbit's velocity almost everywhere in space at every time. For a smooth orbit satisfying the profile integral equation, the formal decay theorem bounds the velocity and its first two spatial derivatives by $C(1+|y|)^{-1-j}$, and the pressure gradient by $C(1+|y|)^{-3}$.

**Paper:** Proposition 7.11, pp.45–47; Lemma 3.6 and Appendix A; Remark 1.2. The paper uses Koch–Nadirashvili–Seregin–Šverák, Proposition 4.1 (2009), and Chae–Wolf, Theorem 1.1 (2017); their hypotheses are met here, as [the statement comparison](paper.md) explains. **Lean:** With the weak-to-mild analytic prerequisites supplied by the assembled proof, `Breakdown.WeakProfile.weakOrbitOfParts_holds`, `Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_holds` and `farFieldDecay_holds` supply the weak-to-mild, smoothing and decay steps through a different proof organization. `Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileExists_of_weak` at [`Breakdown/CertTorus/Main.lean:8`](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/blob/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean/Breakdown/CertTorus/Main.lean#L8) closes weak-to-smooth existence. The authors' existential interfaces hide the correspondence to the originally selected correction; our [Theorem 7.1 wrapper](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/tree/claude/navier-stokes-20261120/lean-wrappers/navier-stokes-theorem71) exposes it, and `Breakdown.theorem71_extended` and `theorem71_cell` prove the full same-witness conclusion with only the standard axioms.

rows.label: sec-11-regularity-of-the-selected-orbit
rows.text: ### 11.1 Proposition II.17: the precise regularity statement **Proposition II.17.** Let $S>0$ and let $\mathcal W\in C(\mathbb R;X)$ be nonzero and period-one. Suppose every term of $T_S\mathcal W+N(\mathcal W)$ is locally integrable and this expression is zero modulo gradients. Then there are smooth $W,q$ satisfying the similarity equation, with period $S$, identity isometry and the profile decay in Theorem II.1, such that $$ W(s,\cdot)=\mathcal W(s/S,\cdot)\quad\text{in }X \quad\text{for every }s\in\mathbb R. \tag{II.51} $$ This is Proposition 7.11, stated on p.44 and proved on pp.45–47. Its hypotheses are much more specific than unrestricted weak Navier–Stokes solvability. The hypotheses of Proposition II.17 already provide a continuous periodic homogeneous $H^1$ orbit. The linked formal weak-profile hypothesis instead gives measurable recurrent fields with global derivative bounds; its construction derives a continuous orbit before smoothing. We verify below how that input reaches each regularity theorem used. ### 11.2 From the similarity equation to a physical mild solution Define, for $t<1$, $$ s=-\log(1-t),\quad \theta=s/S,\quad y=x/\sqrt{1-t}, \qquad u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}\mathcal W(\theta,y). \tag{II.52} $$ Continuity of dilation on $X$ gives $u\in C((-\infty,1);X)$, and the Sobolev embedding gives continuity in $L^6$. Periodicity of $\mathcal W$ implies the uniform scaling bound $$ B_6:=\sup_{t<1}(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_6 =\sup_\theta\|\mathcal W(\theta)\|_6<\infty. \tag{II.53} $$ Changing variables in the weak similarity equation gives the physical weak Navier–Stokes equation against solenoidal tests. In particular, for a compactly supported smooth solenoidal spatial field $\psi$, $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int u(t)\cdot\psi =\int u(t)\cdot\Delta\psi+u(t)\otimes u(t):\nabla\psi. \tag{II.54} $$ Initially this is an identity in time distributions. Both integrals on the right depend continuously on $t$, by $u\in C_tL^6_x$ and the compact support of $\psi$. The left pairing is therefore continuously differentiable and (II.54) holds at every time. We use the weak-to-mild statement proved in Part I, corresponding to the paper's Lemma 3.6: an $X$-continuous solenoidal curve on a compact interval that satisfies (II.54) for every such spatial test is its mild Navier–Stokes evolution from its value at the left endpoint. Consequently, for every $a ### 11.3 Two explicit integrable bootstraps Fix $t<1$, put $h=1-t$, and start (II.55) at $a=t-h$. On $[a,t]$, one has $h\le1-\tau\le2h$, so $\|u(\tau)\|_6\le B_6h^{-1/4}$. The heat kernel maps $L^6$ to $L^{12}$ with bound $Ch^{-1/8}$; the Oseen derivative has $L^{4/3}$ norm at most $Cr^{-7/8}$. These exponents follow from the three-dimensional heat-kernel scaling and one spatial derivative. Since $u\otimes u\in L^3$, Young's and Minkowski's inequalities give $$ \begin{aligned} \|u(t)\|_{12} &\le C h^{-1/8}\|u(a)\|_6 +C\int_a^t(t-\tau)^{-7/8}\|u(\tau)\|_6^2\,d\tau\\ &\le C B_6h^{-3/8}+C B_6^2h^{-1/2}\int_0^h r^{-7/8}\,dr \le C_{B_6}h^{-3/8}. \end{aligned} \tag{II.56} $$ This holds at every $t<1$. Repeat the argument using $L^{12}$ in place of $L^6$. The heat map $L^{12}\to L^\infty$ costs $Ch^{-1/8}$, and $\|\nabla O_r\|_{6/5}\le Cr^{-3/4}$. Since the tensor product is now in $L^6$, $$ \begin{aligned} \|u(t)\|_\infty &\le Ch^{-1/8}\|u(a)\|_{12} +C\int_a^t(t-\tau)^{-3/4}\|u(\tau)\|_{12}^2\,d\tau\\ &\le C_{B_6}h^{-1/2}+C_{B_6}h^{-3/4}\int_0^h r^{-3/4}\,dr \le C'_{B_6}h^{-1/2}. \end{aligned} \tag{II.57} $$ The integrals are $8h^{1/8}$ and $4h^{1/4}$ respectively. Both singularities are integrable; no endpoint convolution estimate is being assumed. Hence $u$ is bounded on every strip $(-\infty,b]\times\mathbb R^3$ with $b<1$. These are the calculations behind (7.63)–(7.65), pp.45–46, using the heat and Oseen estimates established in Part I. ### 11.4 Smoothness, every-time identity and pressure On a compact interval $[a,b]\subset(-\infty,1)$ the solution and its initial datum $u(a)$ are bounded. Since $\|\nabla O_r\|_1\le Cr^{-1/2}$, the nonlinear integral in (II.55) also converges absolutely pointwise on this interval and agrees almost everywhere with the mild expression already obtained. The shifted solution therefore meets the bounded-mild hypotheses of Koch–Nadirashvili–Seregin–Šverák, Proposition 4.1 [K, PDF p.11]: a bounded mild solution with bounded initial datum has bounded distributional derivatives $(t-a)^{j/2+l}\nabla_x^j\partial_t^l u$ for every pair of nonnegative integers $j,l$. It consequently has a smooth representative away from $a$. Since $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary, there is a smooth representative $U$ on the entire interval $(-\infty,1)$. The representative still denotes the original $X$ element at every time. To see this without assuming global gradient continuity for $U$ in advance, fix any compact smooth spatial test $\psi$. The functions $t\mapsto\int u(t)\cdot\psi$ and $t\mapsto\int U(t)\cdot\psi$ are continuous, the first by $C_tL^6$ continuity and the second by local smoothness. Their space-time almost-everywhere equality makes the two continuous pairings equal almost everywhere in time, and therefore everywhere. This holds for all tests, so $U(t)=u(t)$ as spatial distributions at each time. Spatial almost-everywhere equality and uniqueness of weak derivatives transfer the original $L^6$ field and its $L^2$ gradient to $U(t)$. Hence they are equal in $X$ for every time. We henceforth call the smooth representative $u$. Let $G=\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. Equation (II.54) says that this smooth field annihilates every compact solenoidal spatial test at each time. Testing against curls gives $\operatorname{curl}G=0$. On $\mathbb R^3$ the radial primitive $$ p(t,x)=-\int_0^1G(t,\sigma x)\cdot x\,d\sigma \tag{II.58} $$ is smooth and satisfies $\nabla p=-G$. Indeed, differentiating the radial primitive of a curl-free field converts the integrand to the derivative of $\sigma G(t,\sigma x)$; evaluating at $0$ and $1$ gives the required gradient. Thus $(u,p)$ solves the classical physical Navier–Stokes equations. This pressure construction leaves only the usual freedom to add a function of time. ### 11.5 Spatial decay and return to similarity time Periodicity of the original orbit and (II.52) imply, with $\lambda=e^{S/2}>1$, $$ u(1+t,x)=\lambda u(1+\lambda^2t,\lambda x) \qquad(t<0). \tag{II.59} $$ The shifted field is smooth, solves Navier–Stokes and belongs to $C(( -\infty,0);L^6)$, and (II.59) gives ordinary backward discrete self-similarity. These are exactly the hypotheses of Chae–Wolf, Theorem 1.1 [C, PDF p.2], with exponent $p=6$: a smooth backward discretely self-similar solution continuous in $L^p$, for $3\le p<\infty$, obeys a bound by a constant times $(\sqrt{-t}+|x|)^{-1}$. Therefore $$ |u(t,x)|\le\frac{C}{\sqrt{1-t}+|x|},\qquad t<1. \tag{II.60} $$ Now set $$ W(s,y)=e^{-s/2}u(1-e^{-s},e^{-s/2}y), \qquad q(s,y)=e^{-s}p(1-e^{-s},e^{-s/2}y). \tag{II.61} $$ The chain rule gives the similarity equation and solenoidality. The every-time identity already proved gives (II.51), so periodicity and nontriviality are retained. Substitution in (II.60) gives $|W(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-1}$. Here is the derivative-decay step invoked in the paper's Remark 1.2. At a physical point $(t,x)$ choose $r=\frac12\max\{|x|,\sqrt{1-t}\}$. On its backward parabolic cylinder $(t-r^2,t)\times B_r(x)$, either $|x|$ is dominant and $|z|\ge r$, or the time scale is dominant and $\sqrt{1-\tau}\ge2r$. Thus (II.60) bounds $|u|$ by $C/r$ on the cylinder. The pressure-independent interior estimate [V, Lemma 9.1, PDF p.30] states that a smooth Navier–Stokes solution bounded by $A/r$ on a backward cylinder has spatial derivatives of order $j$ bounded by $C_j(A)r^{-j-1}$ on each fixed smaller concentric cylinder. Apply it at the top centre by continuity from earlier times. Since $x=\sqrt{1-t}\,y$ and $$ \nabla_y^jW=(1-t)^{(j+1)/2}\nabla_x^ju, $$ we obtain $|\nabla_y^jW(s,y)|\le C_j(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$, in particular the required first-derivative bound. This finishes Proposition II.17. Its proof uses the exact external regularity statements above, after their hypotheses have been derived. It does not assume finite kinetic energy of the profile. ### 11.6 How the formal regularity proof is organised The formal regularity route proves the necessary analytic results inside the library instead of invoking the two named external profile regularity theorems. The following is a correspondence of proof mechanisms; the complete mathematical proof of Proposition II.17 above follows the published argument. It is not a line-by-line expansion of the much larger far-field library. `Breakdown.WeakProfile.weakOrbitOfParts_holds` produces a continuous mild orbit from the weak profile data. `Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_holds` uses Fourier Sobolev bootstrapping and Picard estimates to obtain a smooth velocity and pressure representing that orbit. Its velocity relation preserves spatial almost-everywhere equality at each time.
